newsitem.title: LATVIA: FEATURE - Baltic economies grow but problems ahead.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Baltic economies grow but problems ahead.

text.p: From the mess and trauma of the fall of the Soviet Union, the Baltic states of Latvia, Lithuania and Estonia have emerged as market economies with steadily rising GDP and falling inflation.
Although they have distinguished themselves from other former Soviet states as strong, committed reformers, each still has problems to be dealt with to ensure future, stable growth.
The three small countries, with a combined population of just under eight million, have also begun to see more economic over-lap with low but increasing investments in each other.
ESTONIA, "BALTIC TIGER" WHICH MAY BE OVER-HEATING

Estonia, which began its push for independence in the late 1980s with requests for more economic autonomy from Moscow, has for some time been seen as the Baltic economic leader. It has even been called the "Baltic Tiger".
It was the only one of the three for which the European Commission recommended the start of early talks for EU entry, saying the country already had a market economy.
Estonian GDP rose four percent in 1996 and inflation in June was 10.8 percent year-on-year.
But success has also sown the seeds of possible problems, with some saying its small economy is over-heating.
"I think there is a consumer boom," said Ardo Hansson, central bank board member and economic advisor to Prime Minister Mart Siimann, forecasting seven percent growth this year.
Economic expansion has been accompanied by a steady rise in the current account deficit to about 12 percent of GDP for the year April 1996 to March 1997.
Lending by banks, benefiting from Estonia's positive image to get cheap funds from abroad, has also been soaring.
Hansson said it grew 62 percent a year in real terms between June 1996 and June 1997.

Ways to rein back the economy are few given the straight-jacket of a currency board, under which the kroon is pegged at eight to one German mark but which removes traditional monetary levers such as interest rate changes.
The authorities have taken some economy-cooling measures such as increased capital adequacy requirements for banks, while the government continues to run a balanced budget.
Hansson said another option being considered was for the government in future to run a budget surplus.
"Right now it all looks very good but sometimes one has to start asking whether the growth number is a good sign or whether we should cool things a little bit," Hansson said.
LATVIA CATCHES UP, POLITICAL FACTOR A WORRY
Latvia, the middle of the three countries both in size and geographical location, has begun to catch up on northern neighbour Estonia after flagging in 1995 and for some of 1996.
Growth was just under three percent in 1996 and inflation lower than Estonia in June at 7.3 percent year-on-year.
Under outgoing prime minister, Andris Shkele, the government drew up a balanced budget and pushed on with a virtually stagnating privatisation programme.
Its international image was also raised under Shkele and the country got a rating from Standard & Poor's that was higher than some central European countries.
One senior Western economist, who declined to be named, said one of Latvia's key problems may now be political instability.
New Prime Minister Guntar Krasts, named on Monday as head of the government, has to control a seven-party coalition that often pulls in different directions.
A convinced reformer himself, he needs to pull the whole, rainbow-coloured cabinet along with him.
"It will be a challenge to stick to tough fiscal policies, particularly with a large current account deficit," the economist said.
He also said Latvia still had to reform its public sector, which was over-blown, inefficient and poorly-administered.
LITHUANIA WEAKNESSES PERSIST
Lithuania, the largest of the Baltic states, has also had the worst problem with image.
The former government of ex-communists, although reformist in words did very little to overhaul the state sector or to privatise industry.
The new right of centre government of Prime Minister Gediminas Vagnorius has begun the process of selling state companies, including Lithuanian Telecom and the airline.
Domenico Fanizza, International Monetary Fund (IMF) representative in Lithuania, said banking was one of the key areas needing reform if it was to support economic development.
Lithuania was shaken in late 1995 by a serious bank crisis that prompted the government to tighten supervision and liquidate some banks rather than save them.
GDP grew in 1996 by 3.6 percent and year-on-year inflation in June was 7.6 percent.

"The same weaknesses still persist: low capitalisation of some of the banks and more generally the bank and financial system does not intermediate and is not geared to the market economy," said Fanizza.
State-owned banks still dominate the market in Lithuania although the government has promised to privatise them.
Bank lending is also very low, with the inter-bank market virtually non-existent.
Expertise in judging the credit worthiness of business projects is also weak, Fanizza added.
He said the government had to improve administration and cut the public sector. Better tax collection and a better use of government funds to encourage investment was also needed.
Although Baltic businessmen look West for markets, they are also looking at each other for investment.
The aggressive Estonians have led the way, with their banks buying into the Latvian market and forming leasing firms in both Latvia and Lithuania.
On a corporate level there is also investment, with an Estonian meat producer and a drugs firm buying into Latvian companies.
